revisions.title: From the city to the guardian
revisions.body: Socrates enlarges the question of justice into a city so its structure can be read at a larger scale. The city begins from non-self-sufficiency, expands through differentiated crafts and exchange, and reaches guardianship as a specialized craft requiring dedicated practice. The guardian is then specified as spirited, gentle toward familiars, and learning-loving. At the endpoint, education is only the next question; tales are classified as true or false.

revisions.title: The first curriculum is selection
revisions.body: Here poetry becomes an instrument of civic design. The discussion puts stories before gymnastics because the young are thought most impressionable at the beginning of education; it therefore refuses random tales and assigns the city the power to approve some stories and reject others. My reading is that this makes education a question of public curation, not private taste.

revisions.title: From imitation to habituation
revisions.body: Here the argument turns representation into habituation. Socrates distinguishes the poet’s own narration from speech performed as another, then applies the one-work principle to mimesis. The question is no longer only what a story depicts, but what a guardian repeatedly practices: imitation can settle into body, voice, and thought. One way to read the turn toward music and gymnastics is as the search for stable formation. At this boundary, the emphasis is formation rather than selection.

revisions.title: From the third wave to a definition of philosophy
revisions.body: Socrates first separates the city’s paradigm from proof that it can be enacted, then narrows the feasibility demand to the nearest possible civic arrangement before stating the philosopher-king condition. The definition that follows makes philosophy a love of wisdom as a whole and of learning itself, not merely of beautiful appearances.

revisions.title: The longer route to the greatest study
revisions.body: Here the dialogue reopens the question of rule by tightening its standard. The discussion of women and children is marked complete, but the rulers’ case must be taken up again; the candidates must combine quick learning with steadiness and survive tests in pleasures, pains, fears, and study. The payoff is methodological: the earlier account of virtue was serviceable but not fully precise, and an incomplete measure cannot measure what it addresses. The “longer route” is therefore a demand for completion, not a decorative detour.

revisions.title: Ascent and civic return
revisions.body: Read the image as a test of orientation, not merely of arrival: the prisoner is forced up a rough ascent, suffers pain, and sees in stages rather than all at once. The movement then turns outward. Socrates assigns the city’s specially educated guardians both contemplation and political work, and links good government to rulers least eager for office. My proposal is that the return tests vision: what one sees must shape how one serves others.

revisions.title: Tyranny as enslavement
revisions.body: Power is turned inside out here. The tyrannized city and tyrannical soul are alike enslaved, so apparent command is not freedom for the whole. Poverty, insatiability, fear, disturbance, and regret mark their condition; the tyrant is pictured as confined, unable to live as free men do. The reversal suggests that command over others does not secure command of oneself. Socrates insists that the judgment requires examination, not mere belief.

revisions.title: A test in images
revisions.body: Rather than simply restating the case for justice, Socrates makes the earlier claim answerable to a picture: a many-headed beast, a lion, and a human are fused beneath one human exterior. He then asks what the advocate of injustice is committed to: strengthening the beast and lion while weakening the human. The image is a device for testing the claim, not a claim that the soul literally has this shape.
